methods-1-1: methods-1-1-1
For the graph of y = (x − 2)²(x + 3), what happens at x = 2?
The graph touches the x-axis and turns
The graph crosses the x-axis without turning
The graph has a stationary point of inflection on the x-axis
The graph has a vertical asymptote
The factor (x − 2) has even multiplicity 2, so the graph touches the x-axis at x = 2 and turns there.
methods-1-1-2
What are the coordinates of the stationary point of inflection of y = (x + 1)³ − 8?
y = a(x − h)³ + k has its stationary point of inflection at (h, k); here h = −1 and k = −8.
methods-1-1-3
What is the y-intercept of y = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3)?
Substituting x = 0 gives (−1)(2)(−3) = 6.
methods-1-1-4
Find the coordinates of the axis intercepts of y = x³ − x² − 6x.
x-intercepts: (−2, 0), (0, 0) and (3, 0); y-intercept: (0, 0).
Factorise: x(x² − x − 6) = x(x − 3)(x + 2). Award marks for correct factorisation and all intercepts.
methods-1-1-5
Which statement describes the end behaviour of y = −2x(x − 1)²(x + 4)?
y → +∞ as x → ±∞
y → +∞ as x → −∞ and y → −∞ as x → +∞
y → −∞ as x → −∞ and y → +∞ as x → +∞
y → −∞ as x → ±∞
The polynomial has degree 4 (even) with leading coefficient −2 (negative), so both ends go down.
methods-1-1-6
Which describes the turning point of y = −(x − 3)⁴ + 2?
A maximum turning point at (3, 2)
A minimum turning point at (3, 2)
A maximum turning point at (−3, 2)
A minimum turning point at (−3, 2)
The graph of y = x⁴ is reflected in the x-axis (so the turning point is a maximum) and translated 3 right and 2 up.
methods-1-1-7
How many x-intercepts does the graph of y = x³ − 4x have?
x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2), giving x-intercepts at x = −2, 0 and 2.
methods-1-1-8
Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points of y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1.
Local maximum at (1, 5) and local minimum at (3, 1).
dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3) = 0 gives x = 1, 3; y(1) = 5, y(3) = 1. For a positive cubic, the first stationary point is the maximum.
methods-1-1-9
A quartic graph touches the x-axis at x = −2, crosses it at x = 1 and x = 4, and has y-intercept 16. Which is its rule?
methods-1-1-10
Where is the local maximum of y = x³ − 3x?
dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1; y(−1) = −1 + 3 = 2, and the graph rises then falls there, so (−1, 2) is the local maximum.
methods-1-1-11
What is the range of y = 2(x − 1)² − 5?
The minimum turning point is (1, −5) and the parabola opens upward, so y ≥ −5 (inclusive).
methods-1-1-12
A cubic has x-intercepts at x = −1, 2 and 4, and a y-intercept of 16. Find its rule.
methods-1-1-13
What is the solution set of x³ − 4x² ≥ 0?
x²(x − 4) ≥ 0. Since x² ≥ 0, we need x − 4 ≥ 0 or x² = 0, so x = 0 or x ≥ 4.
methods-1-1-14
A cubic of the form y = a(x − h)³ + k has a stationary point of inflection at (2, −1) and passes through (3, 1). Which is its rule?
h = 2, k = −1, and 1 = a(1)³ − 1 gives a = 2.
methods-1-1-15
How many real solutions does x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 have?
(x² − 1)(x² − 4) = 0 gives x = ±1 and x = ±2, four distinct real solutions.
methods-1-1-16
Solve x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0 for x ∈ R.
Treat as a quadratic in x²: (x² − 4)(x² − 9) = 0, so x² = 4 or x² = 9.
methods-1-1-17
What is the average rate of change of f(x) = x³ between x = 1 and x = 3?
(f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1) = (27 − 1)/2 = 13. (12 is the instantaneous rate at x = 2.)
methods-1-1-18
For what value of k does the graph of y = x² − 6x + k touch the x-axis exactly once?
A single touching point requires the discriminant 36 − 4k = 0, so k = 9.
methods-1-1-19
What are the coordinates of the turning point of y = x² + 4x + 1?
Completing the square: y = (x + 2)² − 3, so the turning point is (−2, −3).
methods-1-1-20
Find the values of k for which x³ − 3x + k = 0 has three distinct real solutions.
x³ − 3x has a local maximum of 2 at x = −1 and a local minimum of −2 at x = 1. The horizontal line y = −k meets the curve three times when −2 < −k < 2, i.e. −2 < k < 2.
methods-1-1-21
Which statement about the graph of y = −x(x − 2)² is true?
y > 0 for 0 < x < 2
The graph crosses the x-axis at x = 2
y → +∞ as x → +∞
y < 0 for all x > 0 except x = 2
For x > 0, −x is negative and (x − 2)² ≥ 0, so y ≤ 0 with equality only at x = 2, where the graph touches the axis.
methods-1-1-22
What is the solution set of (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 5) < 0?
The positive cubic has roots −2, 1, 5; it is below the x-axis to the left of −2 and between 1 and 5.
methods-1-1-23
What is the maximum number of turning points the graph of a degree 5 polynomial can have?
A polynomial of degree n has at most n − 1 turning points, so a quintic has at most 4.
methods-1-1-24
Describe the behaviour of the graph of y = (x − 1)³(x + 2)² at each of its x-intercepts.
At x = 1 it crosses the x-axis with a stationary point of inflection (odd multiplicity 3). At x = −2 it touches the x-axis and turns (even multiplicity 2).
Link the behaviour to the multiplicity of each factor.
methods-1-1-25

A Bendigo manufacturer makes open boxes from 30 cm × 20 cm sheets of card by cutting a square of side x cm from each corner and folding up the sides. Write the volume V in terms of x and state the domain.
V = x(30 − 2x)(20 − 2x) cm³, with domain 0 < x < 10.
Length 30 − 2x, width 20 − 2x, height x. All dimensions must be positive, so x > 0 and 20 − 2x > 0, giving x < 10.
methods-1-1-c1
For which values of \(k\) does \(x^3 - 3x + k = 0\) have three distinct real solutions?

Stationary points of \(x^3 - 3x + k\) are at \(x = \pm 1\), with values \(k + 2\) (at \(x = -1\)) and \(k - 2\) (at \(x = 1\)). Three roots need the local maximum above 0 and the local minimum below 0: \(k + 2 > 0\) and \(k - 2 < 0\).
methods-1-2: What is the remainder when P(x) = x³ − 2x² + 3x − 5 is divided by x − 2?
By the remainder theorem, the remainder is P(2) = 8 − 8 + 6 − 5 = 1.
Which of the following is a factor of x³ − 7x + 6?
P(−3) = −27 + 21 + 6 = 0, so x + 3 is a factor; the others give P(−1) = P(3) = P(−2) = 12.
If x + 1 is a factor of 2x³ + kx² − 5x + 2, what is the value of k?
Use the factor theorem to show that x − 2 is a factor of P(x) = x³ − 3x² − 6x + 16, and hence factorise P(x) and find all its roots.
P(2) = 8 − 12 − 12 + 16 = 0, so x − 2 is a factor. P(x) = (x − 2)(x² − x − 8), with roots x = 2 and x = (1 ± √33)/2.
Use division or equating coefficients for the quadratic factor, then the quadratic formula: x = (1 ± √(1 + 32))/2.
What is the remainder when 4x³ + x + 2 is divided by 2x − 1?
Which is the full factorisation of x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6?
P(−1) = −1 + 2 + 5 − 6 = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor; dividing gives x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2).
P(x) = x³ + ax + b is divisible by x − 1 and leaves a remainder of 6 when divided by x + 1. Find a and b.
P(1) = 1 + a + b = 0 and P(−1) = −1 − a + b = 6. Adding gives 2b = 6, so b = 3 and a = −4.
P(3) = 54 − 9 − 39 − 6 = 0, so (x − 3) is a factor. Dividing gives 2x² + 5x + 2 = (2x + 1)(x + 2).
What is the quotient when x³ − 8 is divided by x − 2?
Which statement correctly expresses the division of 2x³ + 3x² − x + 5 by x + 1?
Synthetic division by −1 gives coefficients 2, 1, −2 and remainder 7; check P(−1) = −2 + 3 + 1 + 5 = 7.
How many real solutions does x³ − x² + x − 1 = 0 have?
Grouping: x²(x − 1) + (x − 1) = (x − 1)(x² + 1); x² + 1 = 0 has no real solutions, so only x = 1.
P(x) = x³ + ax² + bx + 6. Given x − 1 is a factor of P(x) and the remainder when P(x) is divided by x − 2 is 12, find a and b.
P(1) = 7 + a + b = 0 gives a + b = −7; P(2) = 14 + 4a + 2b = 12 gives 2a + b = −1. Subtracting, a = 6, b = −13.
Which of the following could NOT be a rational root of 2x³ − 3x² + 5x − 6 = 0?
Rational roots p/q must have p dividing 6 and q dividing 2; a denominator of 3 is impossible.
If P(a) = 0 for a polynomial P(x), which statement must be true?
(x − a) is a factor of P(x)
(x + a) is a factor of P(x)
P(x) leaves a remainder of a when divided by x
This is the factor theorem: P(a) = 0 if and only if (x − a) is a factor.
For what value of a does x³ − ax² + 4 leave a remainder of 0 when divided by x − 2?
Find the remainder when 3x⁴ − 2x³ + x − 7 is divided by x + 2.
Given that x − 3 is a factor of x³ − 4x² + x + 6, what is the solution set of x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0?
What is the remainder when x¹⁰⁰ − 1 is divided by x + 1?
When a polynomial P(x) is divided by x − 3, the remainder is 5. What is P(3)?
By the remainder theorem, the remainder on division by x − 3 equals P(3).
Divide x³ + 4x² − 3x + 1 by x − 1, stating the quotient and remainder.
Check the remainder with the remainder theorem: P(1) = 1 + 4 − 3 + 1 = 3.
Which is the factorisation of x³ + 27?
Sum of cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) with a = x, b = 3.
Which is the full factorisation of x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12?
For every real value of k, which is always a factor of P(x) = x³ + kx² + kx + 1?
P(−1) = −1 + k − k + 1 = 0 for all k, so x + 1 is always a factor.
Find m and n such that x² − 1 is a factor of x³ + mx² + nx + 2.
Both x − 1 and x + 1 must be factors: P(1) = 3 + m + n = 0 and P(−1) = 1 + m − n = 0, so m = −2, n = −1. Check: x³ − 2x² − x + 2 = (x − 2)(x² − 1).
Explain why x³ + x + 1 = 0 has no rational solutions.
The only possible rational roots are ±1 (rational root theorem). P(1) = 3 and P(−1) = −1, neither is zero, so there are no rational roots.
Students must identify the candidate roots and test each one.

pieces.text: Let \(p(x) = x^3 + ax^2 - 4x + b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real constants. When \(p(x)\) is divided by \(x - 1\) the remainder is \(-6\), and \(x + 2\) is a factor of \(p(x)\).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Show that \(a = 1\) and \(b = -4\).
pieces.answer: The two conditions give \(a + b = -3\) and \(4a + b = 0\), and solving these simultaneously gives \(a = 1\) and \(b = -4\).

steps.working: Form one equation from each condition. Remainder theorem: \(p(1) = 1 + a - 4 + b = -6\), so \(a + b = -3\). Factor theorem: \(p(-2) = -8 + 4a + 8 + b = 0\), so \(4a + b = 0\).
Subtract the first equation from the second: \(3a = 3\), so \(a = 1\). Then \(b = -3 - a = -4\).

pieces.mistake: Substituting the wrong value: \(p(-1)\) for the divisor \(x - 1\), or \(p(2)\) for the factor \(x + 2\). Substitute the value of \(x\) that makes the divisor zero.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Hence express \(p(x)\) as a product of linear factors.

steps.working: With \(a = 1\) and \(b = -4\), \(p(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 4\). Since \(x + 2\) is a factor, divide (or equate coefficients) to get \(p(x) = (x + 2)(x^2 - x - 2)\).

pieces.mistake: Stopping at \((x + 2)(x^2 - x - 2)\). The question asks for linear factors, so the quadratic must be factorised too.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Hence solve \(p(x) \le 0\).

steps.working: The zeros of \(p\) are \(x = -2, -1, 2\). The leading coefficient is positive, so \(p(x) < 0\) for \(x < -2\), \(p(x) > 0\) on \((-2, -1)\), \(p(x) < 0\) on \((-1, 2)\) and \(p(x) > 0\) for \(x > 2\).
The inequality includes \(p(x) = 0\), so the zeros are included: \(x \in (-\infty, -2] \cup [-1, 2]\).

pieces.mistake: Using round brackets at \(-2\), \(-1\) and \(2\). Those values make \(p(x) = 0\), so they satisfy \(p(x) \le 0\) and belong in the answer.

methods-1-2: When \(P(x)\) is divided by \(x - 1\) the remainder is 3, and when divided by \(x + 2\) the remainder is \(-3\). Find the remainder when \(P(x)\) is divided by \((x - 1)(x + 2)\).
The remainder has degree at most 1: write \(P(x) = (x - 1)(x + 2)Q(x) + ax + b\). Then \(P(1) = a + b = 3\) and \(P(-2) = -2a + b = -3\), so \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\).
methods-1-3: The graph of y = x² is translated 3 units to the right and 2 units up. What is the rule of the image?
A translation of h units right replaces x with x − h; a translation of k units up adds k.
Which is the rule of the image of y = f(x) after a dilation by a factor of 2 from the y-axis?
A dilation by factor a from the y-axis stretches horizontally, replacing x with x/a.
The graph of y = √x is dilated by a factor of 3 from the x-axis. What is the rule of the image?
A dilation by factor 3 from the x-axis multiplies every y-value by 3.
Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of y = √x onto the graph of y = 3√(2 − x).
Reflection in the y-axis, then a translation 2 units right, then a dilation by a factor of 3 from the x-axis.
Check: √x → √(−x) → √(−(x − 2)) = √(2 − x) → 3√(2 − x). Other correct orders are acceptable if the rule is reproduced.
What is the rule of the image of y = e^x after a reflection in the y-axis?
Reflecting in the y-axis replaces x with −x.
The graph of y = 1/x is reflected in the x-axis and then translated 2 units to the left. What is the rule of the image?
Reflecting gives y = −1/x; translating 2 left replaces x with x + 2.
What is the rule of the image of y = x³ after a dilation by a factor of ½ from the y-axis?
The graph of y = x³ is dilated by a factor of 2 from the y-axis, then translated 1 unit left and 4 units down. Find the rule of the image.
Dilation: y = (x/2)³. Translation: replace x with x + 1 and subtract 4.
The graph of y = x² is translated 1 unit up and then dilated by a factor of 2 from the x-axis. What is the rule of the image?
After translating, y = x² + 1; the dilation then doubles all y-values: y = 2(x² + 1) = 2x² + 2.
Which sequence of transformations maps y = x² onto y = −2(x + 1)² + 3?
A dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, a reflection in the x-axis, then a translation 1 unit right and 3 units up
A dilation by factor ½ from the x-axis, a reflection in the y-axis, then a translation 1 unit left and 3 units up
A dilation by factor 2 from the y-axis, a reflection in the x-axis, then a translation 1 unit left and 3 units up
A dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, a reflection in the x-axis, then a translation 1 unit left and 3 units up
The coefficient −2 gives the dilation from the x-axis and the reflection in the x-axis; (x + 1) means 1 unit left; + 3 means 3 units up.
The graph of y = f(x) has a turning point at (2, 5). Where is the corresponding turning point of y = f(x − 1) − 3?
y = f(x − 1) − 3 is a translation 1 unit right and 3 units down, so (2, 5) → (3, 2).
The graph of y = x² is reflected in the x-axis, then translated 3 units up, then dilated by a factor of 2 from the x-axis. Find the rule of the image.
y = −x² → y = −x² + 3 → y = 2(3 − x²) = 6 − 2x². The dilation applies to the whole expression after the translation.
The graph of y = f(x) has an x-intercept at (4, 0). What is the corresponding x-intercept of y = f(2x)?
y = f(2x) is a dilation by factor ½ from the y-axis, so x-coordinates are halved.
Let f(x) = √(x − 1). What is the domain of y = f(−x)?
f(−x) = √(−x − 1) requires −x − 1 ≥ 0, i.e. x ≤ −1. Reflecting in the y-axis maps the domain [1, ∞) to (−∞, −1].
The range of y = f(x) is [0, 4]. What is the range of y = −3f(x) + 1?
The graph of y = f(x) has a turning point at (−1, 4) and a y-intercept at (0, 3). Find the corresponding points on the graph of y = 2f(x + 3) − 1.
What are the equations of the asymptotes of y = 2/(x − 3) + 1?
y = 1/x has asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0; translating 3 right and 1 up moves them to x = 3 and y = 1. The dilation does not change them.
What is the equation of the vertical asymptote of y = log_{e}(x + 2) − 1?
y = log_{e}(x) has asymptote x = 0; translating 2 units left moves it to x = −2.
Which transformation maps y = sin(x) onto y = sin(2x)?
A dilation by a factor of 2 from the y-axis
A dilation by a factor of 2 from the x-axis
A dilation by a factor of ½ from the y-axis
A dilation by a factor of ½ from the x-axis
Replacing x with 2x = x/(½) is a dilation by factor ½ from the y-axis (the period halves to π).
Show that the graph of y = (2x)² can be obtained from y = x² by two different single dilations, and name them.
Since (2x)² = 4x², it is either a dilation by factor ½ from the y-axis or a dilation by factor 4 from the x-axis.
For power functions, a horizontal dilation can be rewritten as an equivalent vertical one.
Dilating y = x² by a factor of 3 from the y-axis gives the same graph as dilating y = x² by what factor from the x-axis?
The horizontal dilation gives y = (x/3)² = (1/9)x², which is a dilation by factor 1/9 from the x-axis.
What is the range of y = 1/(x − 1)² − 2?
1/(x − 1)² takes all values in (0, ∞); subtracting 2 gives (−2, ∞). The asymptote y = −2 is never reached.
The graph of y = e^x is reflected in the x-axis and then translated 4 units up. What is the range of the image?
The image is y = 4 − e^x. Since e^x > 0, y < 4.
Describe the transformations that map y = 1/x onto y = 3/(x − 2) + 1, and state the asymptotes of the image.
Dilation by a factor of 3 from the x-axis, then a translation 2 units right and 1 unit up. Asymptotes: x = 2 and y = 1.
The dilation does not move the asymptotes; the translation moves x = 0 to x = 2 and y = 0 to y = 1.
The graph of y = log_{e}(x) is dilated by a factor of 3 from the y-axis and then reflected in the x-axis. Find the rule of the image and state its domain.
Dilation: y = log_{e}(x/3); reflection in the x-axis multiplies by −1. Equivalently y = log_{e}(3/x). The domain is unchanged because neither transformation affects x-values' sign.
Which sequence of transformations maps the graph of \(y = \sqrt{x}\) onto the graph of \(y = 3\sqrt{2 - x} + 1\)?
Reflection in the \(y\)-axis, translation 2 units right, dilation by factor 3 from the \(x\)-axis, translation 1 unit up
Reflection in the \(y\)-axis, translation 2 units left, dilation by factor 3 from the \(x\)-axis, translation 1 unit up
Reflection in the \(x\)-axis, translation 2 units right, dilation by factor 3 from the \(y\)-axis, translation 1 unit up
Translation 2 units right, reflection in the \(x\)-axis, dilation by factor 3 from the \(x\)-axis, translation 1 unit up

\(\sqrt{x} \to \sqrt{-x}\) (reflect in the \(y\)-axis) \(\to \sqrt{-(x - 2)} = \sqrt{2 - x}\) (2 right) \(\to 3\sqrt{2 - x}\) (dilate from the \(x\)-axis) \(\to +1\) (up 1). Order matters: translating left after the reflection gives \(\sqrt{-x - 2}\).
methods-1-4: Find the image of y = x² under the transformation T(x, y) = (x + 2, 3y).
Let x' = x + 2 and y' = 3y, so x = x' − 2 and y = y'/3. Substituting: y'/3 = (x' − 2)², so y = 3(x − 2)².
What is the image of the point (3, 4) under T(x, y) = (2x, y − 1)?
Which mapping represents a reflection in the x-axis?
Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and negates y.
Find the rule of the image of y = x² under T(x, y) = (x/2 − 1, 3y + 2).
The transformation T(x, y) = (x/2, y) is which of the following?
A dilation by a factor of 2 from the y-axis
A dilation by a factor of ½ from the y-axis
A dilation by a factor of ½ from the x-axis
A dilation by a factor of 2 from the x-axis
Multiplying x-coordinates by ½ halves distances from the y-axis.
Find the image of y = √x under T(x, y) = (−x, 2y + 1).
Which transformation maps y = x² onto y = (x − 1)² + 5?
The image is the parabola translated 1 unit right and 5 units up, so add 1 to x and 5 to y.
Find a transformation T, written as T(x, y) = (…, …), that maps y = √x onto y = 1 − √(x + 3).
Reflect in the x-axis, then translate 3 left and 1 up. Check: x = x' + 3 and y = 1 − y', so 1 − y' = √(x' + 3), giving y' = 1 − √(x' + 3).
Under T(x, y) = (3x − 1, −y + 2), which point maps to (5, −4)?
Solve 3x − 1 = 5, giving x = 2, and −y + 2 = −4, giving y = 6. (14, 6) is the image of (5, −4), not its pre-image.
The transformation [x'; y'] = [[2, 0], [0, −1]][x; y] + [0; 3] (rows separated by semicolons) is equivalent to which mapping?
Multiplying out gives x' = 2x and y' = −y, then adding the translation vector gives y' = −y + 3.
Find the image of y = e^x under T(x, y) = (x − 3, 2y).
x = x' + 3 and y = y'/2, so y'/2 = e^(x' + 3), giving y = 2e^(x + 3).
Find a transformation that maps y = 2(x + 1)² − 3 back onto y = x².
The forward mapping from y = x² is (x, y) → (x − 1, 2y − 3); its inverse is (x, y) → (x + 1, (y + 3)/2). Check: y' = (y + 3)/2 = (x + 1)² = x'².
Which transformation maps y = x³ onto y = 8x³?
With x' = x/2, x = 2x', so y' = (2x')³ = 8x'³.
Find the image of the line y = 2x + 1 under T(x, y) = (x, 3y).
y = y'/3 and x = x', so y'/3 = 2x' + 1, giving y = 6x + 3.
What is the domain of the image of y = log_{e}(x) under T(x, y) = (−x, y + 4)?
The original domain x > 0 maps to x' = −x < 0. The vertical translation does not affect the domain.
A transformation is a dilation by a factor of 2 from the y-axis, then a reflection in the x-axis, then a translation 3 units left. Write it in mapping notation and in matrix form.
The diagonal entries give the dilation and reflection; the translation vector gives the shift.
The point (−1, 2) is a turning point of y = f(x). What is the corresponding turning point after T(x, y) = (2x + 1, y − 3)?
What is the inverse of the transformation T(x, y) = (2x + 4, y − 1)?
Undo each step in reverse order: subtract 4 then halve for x, and add 1 for y.
Find the image of y = 1/x under T(x, y) = (x, −2y).
y = −y'/2 and x = x', so −y'/2 = 1/x', giving y = −2/x.
Find the rule and the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the image of y = e^x under T(x, y) = (2x, y + 1).
x = x'/2 and y = y' − 1, so y' − 1 = e^(x'/2). The asymptote y = 0 moves up 1 unit.
Which mapping takes the graph of y = f(x) onto the graph of y = f(x + 5) − 2?
y = f(x + 5) − 2 is a translation 5 units left and 2 units down.
What is the period of the image of y = sin(x) under T(x, y) = (3x, y)?
The image is y = sin(x/3), a horizontal stretch by factor 3, so the period becomes 3 × 2π = 6π.
What are the asymptotes of the image of y = 1/x under T(x, y) = (x + 1, 2y − 3)?
The image is y = 2/(x − 1) − 3. The asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0 map to x = 1 and y = 2(0) − 3 = −3.
Compare the images of y = f(x) under T₁(x, y) = (2x + 2, y) and T₂(x, y) = (2(x + 2), y).

T₁ gives y = f((x − 2)/2); T₂ gives y = f((x − 4)/2). T₁ is a dilation by factor 2 from the y-axis then a translation 2 right; T₂ is a translation 2 right then the dilation (total shift 4 right), so the images differ by 2 units horizontally.
The order of dilation and translation changes the result.
Find values of a, b, c and d such that T(x, y) = (ax + b, cy + d) maps y = x³ onto y = 1 − (2x − 4)³.
One possible answer: a = ½, b = 2, c = −1, d = 1.

methods-6-3.title: Area between a parabola and a line

pieces.text: The graphs of \(f(x) = 4x - x^2\) and \(g(x) = x\) intersect at two points.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the coordinates of the two points of intersection.

steps.working: Use \(g(x) = x\) for the \(y\)-coordinates: the points are \((0, 0)\) and \((3, 3)\).

pieces.mistake: Dividing both sides of \(x^2 - 3x = 0\) by \(x\), which loses the solution \(x = 0\). Factorise instead.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Write down a definite integral whose value is the area of the region enclosed by the two graphs.

steps.working: On \([0, 3]\) the parabola is above the line (for example \(f(1) = 3 > g(1) = 1\)), so the area is \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\,dx = \int_0^3 (3x - x^2)\,dx\).

pieces.mistake: Subtracting the wrong way round. \(\int_0^3 \big(g(x) - f(x)\big)\,dx\) is negative; subtract the lower graph from the upper one.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Hence find the area of the region.
pieces.mistake: Writing the antiderivative of \(3x\) as \(3x^2\) instead of \(\frac{3x^2}{2}\). Add one to the power, then divide by the new power.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain why the line \(x = \frac{3}{2}\) divides the region into two parts of equal area.
pieces.answer: The height of the region, \(3x - x^2\), is symmetric about \(x = \frac{3}{2}\), so the two parts have the same height at equal distances from that line and each has area \(\frac{9}{4}\).

steps.working: The vertical height of the region at \(x\) is \(h(x) = f(x) - g(x) = 3x - x^2 = x(3 - x)\), a parabola with zeros at \(0\) and \(3\), so its axis of symmetry is \(x = \frac{3}{2}\).

Since \(h(3 - x) = (3 - x)x = h(x)\), the height at \(\frac{3}{2} - t\) equals the height at \(\frac{3}{2} + t\). So \(\displaystyle\int_0^{3/2} h(x)\,dx = \int_{3/2}^{3} h(x)\,dx = \frac{9}{4}\), which is half of \(\frac{9}{2}\).

pieces.mistake: Saying the region itself is symmetric about \(x = \frac{3}{2}\). It is not, because the line \(y = x\) slopes; what is symmetric is the vertical distance between the two graphs.

pieces.text: At a bakery, 20% of customers buy a pie. A random sample of 12 customers is taken, and \(X\) is the number of them who buy a pie. Assume that customers decide independently of each other.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr(X = 3)\), correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Leaving out the \(\binom{12}{3}\) factor. It counts the 220 different ways that 3 of the 12 customers can be the ones who buy a pie.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr(X \ge 2)\), correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Calculating \(1 - \Pr(X \le 2)\), which is \(\Pr(X > 2)\). 'At least 2' includes 2, so subtract only \(\Pr(X = 0)\) and \(\Pr(X = 1)\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr(X \ge 2 \mid X \le 4)\), correct to four decimal places.

steps.working: With CAS, \(\Pr(2 \le X \le 4) \approx 0.65257\) and \(\Pr(X \le 4) \approx 0.92744\), so the probability is \(\dfrac{0.65257}{0.92744} \approx 0.7036\).

pieces.mistake: Putting \(\Pr(X \ge 2)\) in the numerator. The numerator is the probability that both events happen, \(\Pr(2 \le X \le 4)\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the smallest number of customers that must be sampled so that the probability that at least one of them buys a pie is greater than 0.99.

steps.working: \(n > \dfrac{\log_e 0.01}{\log_e 0.8} \approx 20.64\), so the smallest sample size is \(n = 21\).

pieces.mistake: Rounding \(20.64\) down to \(20\). Check: \(0.8^{20} \approx 0.0115\) is still above \(0.01\), so 20 customers is not enough.

A and B are independent events with Pr(A) = 0.3 and Pr(B) = 0.6. Find Pr(A ∩ B).
For independent events Pr(A ∩ B) = Pr(A)Pr(B) = 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18.
methods-7-4-5
A and B are mutually exclusive events with Pr(A) = 0.3 and Pr(B) = 0.5. Find Pr(A ∪ B).
Mutually exclusive events have Pr(A ∩ B) = 0, so Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8.

A and B are mutually exclusive events, each with non-zero probability. Which statement is true?
A and B are always independent
A and B are independent only if Pr(A) = Pr(B)
A and B are independent if Pr(A) + Pr(B) = 1

Pr(A ∩ B) = 0 but Pr(A)Pr(B) > 0, so the independence condition can never hold.

Pr(A) = 0.4 and Pr(B | A) = 0.25. Find Pr(A ∩ B).

For events A and B with Pr(B) > 0, the statement Pr(A | B) = Pr(A) means that
A and B are mutually exclusive
A and B are independent
B is a subset of A
A′ and B are mutually exclusive
If knowing B occurred does not change the probability of A, the events are independent by definition.
methods-7-4-9
A bag contains 5 red and 3 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
Pr(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. (25/64 wrongly assumes replacement.)

A bag contains 5 red and 3 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given the first ball is green, find the probability that the second ball is red.
After removing a green ball, 5 of the remaining 7 balls are red, so the probability is 5/7.

methods-7-4-13

Explain the difference between mutually exclusive events and independent events.

Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so Pr(A ∩ B) = 0. Independent events do not affect each other's probabilities, so Pr(A ∩ B) = Pr(A)Pr(B). Events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both.

In a random sample of 500 Victorian adults, 160 had received a flu vaccination this year. An approximate 95% confidence interval for p is closest to
Using the same sample data, an approximate 90% confidence interval for p compared with an approximate 95% interval is
the same width, with a different centre
Both intervals are centred at p̂. The smaller z-value (1.645 rather than 1.96) gives a narrower interval.

In a random sample of 600 VCE students, 390 had a part-time job. Find an approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all VCE students with a part-time job, with endpoints correct to three decimal places.
Find p̂ first, then the margin of error.
A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of Victorians who walk daily is (0.47, 0.55). Interpret this interval.

If many random samples of the same size were taken and an interval constructed from each, about 95% of these intervals would contain the true proportion p. This interval gives plausible values of p from 0.47 to 0.55.
Do not say there is a 95% probability that p lies in this particular interval.
In a random sample of 250 people, p̂ = 0.4. Find the margin of error for an approximate 90% confidence interval, correct to three decimal places.
A preliminary estimate gives p̂ = 0.2. Find the smallest sample size needed so that the margin of error of an approximate 95% confidence interval is at most 0.04.
Always round the sample size up.
An approximate 95% confidence interval for p is (0.52, 0.60). Find p̂, the margin of error, and the approximate sample size used.
p̂ is the midpoint and M is half the width.
A water authority claims that 70% of residents support water restrictions. A survey gives an approximate 95% confidence interval of (0.61, 0.67). Comment on the claim.
0.70 is outside the interval, so the survey gives evidence that the true proportion is less than 70% and does not support the claim.
Base the conclusion on whether the claimed value lies inside the interval.
Explain why the confidence interval p̂ ± z√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) is described as approximate.
It uses the normal approximation to the distribution of P̂. It also uses p̂ in place of the unknown p when calculating the standard deviation.
To halve the width of an approximate 95% confidence interval for \(p\) (with the same \(\hat{p}\)), the sample size must be:
The width is proportional to \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\), so halving it requires \(\sqrt{n}\) to double, i.e. \(n\) to be multiplied by 4.
methods-challenge: Find the value of \(k\) for which the line \(y = kx\) is a tangent to the curve \(y = e^x\), and the point of contact.
At the contact point \(x = a\): the gradients match (\(e^a = k\)) and the line passes through the point (\(e^a = ka\)). So \(ka = k\), giving \(a = 1\) and \(k = e\).
The area enclosed by \(y = x^2\) and \(y = 2x - x^2\) is:
Let \(f(x) = (x - a)^2(x - b)\) where \(a < b\). The \(x\)-coordinate of the local minimum is:

\(f'(x) = (x - a)\big[2(x - b) + (x - a)\big] = (x - a)(3x - a - 2b)\). The repeated root \(x = a\) is a local maximum (a positive cubic touches from above), so the minimum is at \(x = \frac{a + 2b}{3}\).
Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum is 8, the probability that at least one die shows a 6 is:
Sum 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), five equally likely outcomes, two of which include a 6.
A random variable has density \(f(x) = \dfrac{k}{x}\) for \(1 \le x \le e\). Find \(k\) and \(\text{E}(X)\).
For \(f(x) = x^3\) and \(a > 0\), find \(c \in (0, a)\) where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over \([0, a]\).
Average rate \(= \frac{a^3 - 0}{a} = a^2\). \(f'(c) = 3c^2 = a^2\), so \(c = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\) (the positive value in \((0, a)\)).
Let \(f(x) = 2x^3 + 1\). The gradient of the graph of \(y = f^{-1}(x)\) at \(x = 3\) is:
\(f(1) = 3\), so \(f^{-1}(3) = 1\). The inverse's gradient is the reciprocal: \(\frac{1}{f'(1)} = \frac{1}{6}\).
Each trial succeeds with probability 0.1, independently. Find the least number of trials so that the probability of at least one success exceeds 0.95.
\(1 - 0.9^n > 0.95\), so \(0.9^n < 0.05\) and \(n > \frac{\log_e 0.05}{\log_e 0.9} \approx 28.4\). The least whole number is 29 (dividing by a negative log reverses the inequality).
How many solutions does \(\sin(2x) = \frac{1}{2}\) have for \(x \in [0, 2\pi]\)?
\(2x \in [0, 4\pi]\) covers two full periods; each period has two solutions of \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\), giving 4.

X.title: A cubic curve and a probability density function
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA Exam 2, Section B

pieces.text: Let \(f: [0, 3] \to \mathbb{R}\), \(f(x) = x(x - 3)^2\). The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is shown below.

diagram.alt: Graph of y = f(x) for x from 0 to 3. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a single peak, then falls to touch the x-axis at x = 3.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Show that \(f'(x) = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)\).

steps.working: Product rule with \(u = x\) and \(v = (x - 3)^2\): \(f'(x) = (x - 3)^2 + x \times 2(x - 3)\).

pieces.mistake: Writing only the final line. In a 'show that' question the working is the answer, so show the product rule (or the expanded form \(x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x\)) before factorising.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of \(f\) in the interval \((0, 3)\), and state its nature.

steps.working: \(f'(0.5) = 3(-0.5)(-2.5) > 0\) and \(f'(2) = 3(1)(-1) < 0\), so the gradient changes from positive to negative and \((1, 4)\) is a local maximum.

pieces.mistake: Stating 'maximum' with no reason. Support it with a sign test of \(f'\) on either side of \(x = 1\), or with \(f''(1) = -6 < 0\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of \(f\) at the point where \(x = 2\).
pieces.mistake: Using \(f(2)\) as the gradient. The gradient is \(f'(2)\); \(f(2)\) gives the point that the tangent passes through.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the area of the region enclosed by the graph of \(f\) and the \(x\)-axis.

steps.working: \(f(x) \ge 0\) on \([0, 3]\) and \(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x\), so the area is \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 (x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x)\,dx\).

pieces.mistake: Antidifferentiating \(x(x - 3)^2\) factor by factor, as \(\frac{x^2}{2} \times \frac{(x - 3)^3}{3}\). There is no product rule for antiderivatives, so expand first.

pieces.text: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \[g(x) = \begin{cases} k\,x(x - 3)^2 & 0 \le x \le 3 \\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}\] where \(k\) is a positive constant.

pieces.label: e.i
pieces.question: Show that \(k = \frac{4}{27}\).
pieces.answer: The total area under a probability density function is 1. Using part d, \(\frac{27}{4}k = 1\), so \(k = \frac{4}{27}\).

steps.working: \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 k\,x(x - 3)^2\,dx = 1\). By part d, \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 x(x - 3)^2\,dx = \frac{27}{4}\), so \(\frac{27}{4}k = 1\) and \(k = \frac{4}{27}\).

pieces.mistake: Setting the maximum value of \(g\), which is \(4k\), equal to 1. It is the area under the graph, not its height, that must equal 1.

pieces.label: e.ii
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr(X < 1)\).
pieces.mistake: Leaving out \(k\) and giving \(\frac{11}{4}\). A probability can never be greater than 1.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find \(\text{E}(X)\).
pieces.mistake: Integrating \(g(x)\) instead of \(x\,g(x)\). That integral is always 1, the total probability.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: Find the median of \(X\), correct to three decimal places.

steps.working: The median \(m\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_0^m g(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\), that is, \(\frac{4}{27}\left(\frac{m^4}{4} - 2m^3 + \frac{9m^2}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\) with \(0 \le m \le 3\).
Solve with CAS. The quartic has two real solutions, \(m \approx -0.742\) and \(m \approx 1.157\). Only the second lies in \([0, 3]\), so the median is \(1.157\).

pieces.mistake: Reporting a CAS solution that lies outside \([0, 3]\). The median must be in the interval where the density is defined.

X.title: Seedlings in a nursery
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA Exam 2, Section B

pieces.text: A nursery grows seedlings. The height, \(h\) cm, of a typical seedling \(t\) weeks after it is planted is modelled by \(h(t) = 20 - 18e^{-0.25t}\), \(t \ge 0\).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the height of a seedling when it is planted.
pieces.mistake: Taking \(e^0\) to be 0. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the rate at which the height is increasing when \(t = 4\), in cm per week, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Giving the height \(h(4) \approx 13.38\) cm. A rate of change needs the derivative \(h'(t)\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find how long after planting a seedling reaches a height of 15 cm. Give your answer in weeks, correct to one decimal place.
pieces.mistake: Taking logs before the exponential term is on its own, for example writing \(\log_e(20 - 18e^{-0.25t})\) as \(\log_e 20 - \log_e(18e^{-0.25t})\). There is no log law for a difference inside the log.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: State the height that the model predicts seedlings approach in the long term.

steps.working: As \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{-0.25t} \to 0\), so \(h(t) \to 20\). The model predicts heights approach 20 cm.

pieces.mistake: Answering 18 cm, the coefficient of the exponential term. That term shrinks to 0, which leaves 20.

pieces.text: Seeds are sown in trays of 10. Each seed germinates with probability 0.9, independently of the others. Let \(Y\) be the number of seeds in a tray that germinate.

pieces.label: e.i
pieces.question: Find the probability that all 10 seeds in a tray germinate, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Calculating \(1 - 0.9^{10}\), which is the probability that at least one seed fails to germinate.

pieces.label: e.ii
pieces.question: Find the probability that at least 8 seeds in a tray germinate, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Leaving out \(\Pr(Y = 8)\), which gives \(\Pr(Y > 8)\). 'At least 8' includes 8.

pieces.text: Individual seedlings vary. Ten weeks after planting, the heights of the seedlings are normally distributed with mean 18.5 cm and standard deviation 0.8 cm.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find the proportion of seedlings that are taller than 20 cm ten weeks after planting, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Entering the variance, \(0.64\), where the calculator asks for the standard deviation, \(0.8\).

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: In a random sample of 200 seedlings, 174 were ready for sale. Find an approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all the nursery's seedlings that are ready for sale. Give the end points correct to three decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Using \(n = 174\) in the standard error. Here \(n\) is the sample size, 200.

X.title: A sine curve and a probability
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA Exam 1

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Solve \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}\).
pieces.mistake: Forgetting to halve, or giving only the first-quadrant solution. Sine is also positive in the second quadrant, so \(\theta = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6}\) is a solution too.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the gradient of the graph of \(f\) at \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
pieces.mistake: Writing \(f'(x) = \cos(2x)\). By the chain rule, the derivative of \(\sin(2x)\) is \(2\cos(2x)\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the area of the region enclosed by the graph of \(f\) and the \(x\)-axis for \(0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\).
pieces.mistake: Antidifferentiating \(\sin(2x)\) as \(-2\cos(2x)\). Divide by the 2 instead of multiplying: the antiderivative is \(-\frac{1}{2}\cos(2x)\).

pieces.text: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \[g(x) = \begin{cases} k\sin(2x) & 0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2} \\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}\] where \(k\) is a positive constant.

pieces.label: d.i
pieces.question: Show that \(k = 1\).
pieces.answer: The total area under a probability density function is 1. By part c, \(\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin(2x)\,dx = 1\), so \(k \times 1 = 1\) and \(k = 1\).

steps.working: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} k\sin(2x)\,dx = 1\). By part c the integral of \(\sin(2x)\) over this interval is 1, so \(k = 1\).

pieces.mistake: Setting the maximum value of \(g\) equal to 1. That happens to give \(k = 1\) here as well, but the reason is that the area under \(g\) must be 1.

pieces.label: d.ii
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr\left(X < \frac{\pi}{6}\right)\).
pieces.mistake: Evaluating \(\cos\) at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) instead of at \(2 \times \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

pieces.label: d.iii
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr\left(X < \frac{\pi}{6} \mid X < \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\).

steps.working: The event \(X < \frac{\pi}{6}\) lies inside \(X < \frac{\pi}{4}\), so the probability is \(\dfrac{\Pr\left(X < \frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{\Pr\left(X < \frac{\pi}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{1/4}{1/2} = \frac{1}{2}\).

pieces.mistake: Multiplying the two probabilities as if the events were independent. For a conditional probability, divide the probability of both events by the probability of the given event.

X.title: A cooling cup of coffee
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA Exam 2, Section B

pieces.text: The temperature of a cup of coffee, \(T\) °C, \(t\) minutes after it is poured is modelled by \(T(t) = 20 + 70e^{-0.1t}\), \(t \ge 0\).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the temperature of the coffee when it is poured.
pieces.mistake: Writing 70 °C. The coffee starts at \(20 + 70\), not 70.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the rate at which the temperature is changing 5 minutes after the coffee is poured, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Dropping the negative sign. A falling temperature has a negative rate of change.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find how long it takes for the coffee to cool to 60 °C, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Solving \(70e^{-0.1t} = 60\) and forgetting the room temperature of 20.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the average temperature of the coffee over the first 10 minutes, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Averaging the starting and finishing temperatures. That is only correct for linear change; use the average value of the function.

pieces.text: At a café, the serving temperature of coffees is normally distributed with mean 75 °C and standard deviation 4 °C.

pieces.label: e.i
pieces.question: Find the probability that a randomly chosen coffee is served below 70 °C, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Using the variance (16) instead of the standard deviation (4) in the calculator.

pieces.label: e.ii
pieces.question: Find the temperature \(c\) such that 90% of coffees are served hotter than \(c\) °C, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Using 0.9 in the inverse normal, which gives the temperature that 90% are below.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: A customer orders 5 coffees. Assuming their temperatures are independent, find the probability that exactly 2 are served below 70 °C, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Rounding the probability from part e.i to 0.1 before using it, which changes the fourth decimal place.

X.title: A logarithm and its inverse
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA Exam 1

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the rule and domain of the inverse function \(f^{-1}\).

steps.working: The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), which is \(\mathbb{R}\).

pieces.mistake: Giving the domain of \(f\), \((-1, \infty)\). The inverse's domain is the original function's range.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the gradient of the graph of \(f\) at \(x = 1\).
pieces.mistake: Writing \(f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x + 1}\) and forgetting the coefficient 2.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of \(f\) at the origin.
pieces.mistake: Using \(f'(1)\) from part b. The tangent at the origin needs the gradient at \(x = 0\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Solve \(f(x) = 2\).

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the exact area of the region enclosed by the graph of \(y = f^{-1}(x)\), the \(x\)-axis and the line \(x = 2\).

steps.working: \(f^{-1}(0) = 0\) and \(f^{-1}(x) \ge 0\) for \(x \ge 0\), so the area is \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 \left(e^{x/2} - 1\right)dx = \Big[2e^{x/2} - x\Big]_0^2\).

pieces.mistake: Antidifferentiating \(e^{x/2}\) as \(\frac{1}{2}e^{x/2}\). Dividing by the coefficient \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(2e^{x/2}\).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is dilated by a factor of 2 from the \(y\)-axis and then translated 1 unit in the positive direction of the \(x\)-axis. Find the rule of the image.

steps.working: Dilation by factor 2 from the \(y\)-axis replaces \(x\) with \(\frac{x}{2}\): \(y = 2\log_e\left(\frac{x}{2} + 1\right)\).

pieces.mistake: Replacing \(x\) with \(2x\) for a dilation by factor 2 from the \(y\)-axis. Dilating by factor \(k\) replaces \(x\) with \(\frac{x}{k}\).

X.title: Challenge: a family of cubics
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of VCAA Exam 2, Section B

pieces.text: Let \(f(x) = x^3 - 3a^2x\), where \(a\) is a positive constant.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of \(f\), in terms of \(a\), and state their nature.

steps.working: \(f(-a) = 2a^3\) (local maximum) and \(f(a) = -2a^3\) (local minimum), as for any positive cubic.

pieces.mistake: Forgetting that \(a\) is a constant and differentiating \(a^2\) too.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the value of \(a\) for which the local maximum lies on the line \(y = 16\).
pieces.mistake: Using the local minimum value.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Show that the tangent to the graph of \(f\) at \(x = 2a\) has equation \(y = 9a^2x - 16a^3\).
pieces.mistake: Substituting \(x = 2a\) into \(f'\) incorrectly as \(3(2a)^2 = 6a^2\). Square the whole \(2a\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the \(x\)-coordinate of the other point where this tangent meets the graph of \(f\).

steps.working: \(x = 2a\) is a double root (the tangent touches there): \((x - 2a)^2(x + 4a) = 0\), so the other point is \(x = -4a\).

pieces.mistake: Not using the known double root. The tangent point is always a repeated root of the equation.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the area enclosed by the graph of \(f\) and the \(x\)-axis for \(0 \le x \le \sqrt{3}\,a\), in terms of \(a\).

steps.working: \(f(x) \le 0\) on \([0, \sqrt{3}a]\), so the area is \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{3}a} (3a^2x - x^3)\,dx = \left[\frac{3a^2x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt{3}a}\).

pieces.mistake: Integrating \(f\) directly and getting a negative answer. Area below the axis needs the integral of \(-f\).

pieces.text: For \(a = 1\), let \(g(x) = k(3x - x^3)\) for \(0 \le x \le \sqrt{3}\) (and 0 elsewhere) be a probability density function.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find \(k\).

steps.working: By part e with \(a = 1\), \(\int_0^{\sqrt{3}} (3x - x^3)\,dx = \frac{9}{4}\), so \(k = \frac{4}{9}\).

pieces.mistake: Setting the maximum of \(g\) equal to 1 instead of the area.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: Find \(\Pr(X < 1)\).
pieces.mistake: Forgetting the factor \(k\).

X.title: Challenge: a bottling machine
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of VCAA Exam 2, Section B

pieces.text: A machine fills bottles with volume \(V\) mL, where \(V\) is normally distributed with mean 500 mL and standard deviation 4 mL. A bottle is rejected if it holds less than 495 mL or more than 508 mL.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the probability that a bottle is rejected, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Finding only one tail. A bottle is rejected for being too low or too high.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Given that a bottle is rejected, find the probability it was underfilled, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Multiplying instead of dividing.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Bottles are packed in twelves. Find the probability that at most one bottle in a pack is rejected, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Rounding \(p\) to 0.13 too early, which changes the fourth decimal place.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: The mean is adjusted (standard deviation unchanged) so that only 2% of bottles hold less than 495 mL. Find the new mean, correct to two decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Using \(+2.0537\), which puts the mean below 495.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: In a random sample of 200 bottles from a second machine, 30 were underfilled. Find an approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion of underfilled bottles, correct to four decimal places.
pieces.mistake: Using \(n = 30\) instead of the sample size, 200.
